/// writes the formatter implementation for <c>T</c>, even when <c>T</c> is declared in another assembly that cannot reference MessagePack.
/// The formatted type <c>T</c> is serialized in contractless mode: every public, non-static, read-write instance property and field

/// Surrogate members are matched to members of <c>T</c> by name.
/// Gets or sets a type whose <see cref="KeyAttribute"/> members define the keys and membership of the formatted type.
/// Each surrogate member that carries a <see cref="KeyAttribute"/> must match a public, read-write instance member of the formatted type by name.
/// Surrogate members that carry <see cref="IgnoreMemberAttribute"/> are excluded.
/// All keys in the surrogate must be the same kind (all integer or all string).

sources.text:
Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack
    
I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

Therefore, in the usual scenario, it will work with AOT Safe without any special handling. If you prefer to restrict your resolver to source-generated formatters, you should use the `MessagePack.GeneratedMessagePackResolver`, which is source generated into your project for that purpose. This type's name and namespace can be customized by applying `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` to a `partial class` that you define, at which point that class becomes the resolver for you to use. At runtime, if a source generated or hand-written formatter cannot be found for a given `[MessagePackObject]` type, MessagePack will generate the formatters on the fly using [Reflection.Emit](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.ilgenerator) to create highly-tuned formatters for each type. This code generation has a minor upfront performance cost. > Note: When using Unity, dynamic code generation only works when targeting .NET Framework 4.x + mono runtime. For all other Unity targets, AOT is required. ### Customizations You can customize the generated source through properties on the `GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute`. ```cs [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class MyResolver { } ``` When exposing the generated resolver publicly, consumers outside the library should aggregate the resolver using its `Instance` property, which contains *only* the generated formatters. Two assembly-level attributes exist to help with mixing in your own custom formatters with the automatically generated ones: - `MessagePackKnownFormatterAttribute` - `MessagePackAssumedFormattableAttribute` Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer). ### MagicOnion [MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL. ### StreamJsonRpc The StreamJsonRpc library is based on [JSON-RPC](https://www.jsonrpc.org/) and includes [a pluggable formatter architecture](https://github.com/microsoft/vs-streamjsonrpc/blob/master/doc/extensibility.md#alternative-formatters) and as of v2.3 includes [MessagePack support](https://github.com/microsoft/vs-streamjsonrpc/blob/master/doc/extensibility.md#message-formatterss). ## How to build See our [contributor's guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Code of Conduct This project has adopted the code of conduct defined by the Contributor Covenant to clarify expected behavior in our community. For more information see the [.NET Foundation Code of Conduct](https://dotnetfoundation.org/code-of-conduct). ## .NET Foundation This project is supported by the [.NET Foundation](https://dotnetfoundation.org).
